1:
The revolt breaks before the last one has cooled. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) marks the timing as the lesson: it follows immediately on the crushing of Absalom, so that the end of one trouble proves the beginning of another, and a reconciliation newly made needed handling tenderly, a broken bone once set requiring time to knit. He traces the occasion to the quarrel over who had most interest in bringing the king home, Israel pleading their numbers and Judah their kinship; David inclined to his own tribe, and when Israel saw it they flew off. From that he draws a cluster of warnings — that partiality is as impolitic in a prince as in a parent, that the hatred of inferiors may be feared whose love is despised, that the beginning of strife is as the letting forth of water (Prov. 17:14), and that the perverting of words is the subverting of peace, since Judah said only that the king was near of kin and Israel heard in it that they had no part in him.

On the man himself the witnesses divide over a word. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that the English follows the ancient versions in taking Bichri for a proper name, whereas most recent commentators read it as a patronymic, the Bichrite, of the family of Becher the second son of Benjamin — which would make him of Saul's clan by descent rather than by tribe only. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reaches Saul's family by the looser route, inferring it from his being a Benjamite, and confesses nothing further is known of him. Henry adds that Shimei and he were both of Saul's tribe and both kept the old grudge of that house. Ellicott also hears in the cry to the tents the very signal Jeroboam would later use (1 Kings 12:16). John Gill (reformed) and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agree that the man's being on the spot was chance in its second causes and providence in its first, Gill tying it to the standing threat that the sword should not depart from David's house.

Ellicott then states the reversal plainly: Judah, among whom the rebellion had originated and who had been slow to return to their allegiance, were now fierce in loyalty, while Israel, who had merely joined an organised revolt and had afterwards been first to propose the king's return, had become the alienated party. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) guard against over-reading the geography: that Judah clave to him from Jordan does not prove the revolt broke out at the river before David reached Gilgal, since the phrase is explained by Judah having already fetched him across.

The ten concubines divide them four ways, and the question is whether the women were at fault. Henry holds they were, and makes the confinement a punishment for an easy submission to Absalom's lust, laid alongside two other obligations — duty, since they were now unclean to David, and prudence, that the thing might not be so much as named (1 Cor. 5:1). Clarke denies it: they were not in the transgression, so he could not punish them, nor divorce them, nor be familiar with them again, nor safely marry them elsewhere, so he shut them up and fed them and made them quite comfortable. Keil and Delitzsch read the act as protective, that he brought them into a place of safety and took care of them. Ellicott makes it neither punishment nor kindness but arithmetic, the necessary result under polygamy of what had happened. On the phrase for their state he allows the received widowhood of life or, with the Chaldee, widowhood of the living — widows while their husband still lived; Keil and Delitzsch keep the former.
4:
The commission to Amasa begins to pay a promise, and nearly everyone thinks it ill-timed. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) call this first step toward fulfilment a very imprudent act, like the promise itself, since Joab had commanded for years and was grievously offended, and a well-tried general had incomparably more standing in Judah than a man who had led Absalom's rebel army could have. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) agrees more briefly, calling it of very doubtful expediency at such a crisis. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sees both sides: the revolt let David keep his word sooner than he could have wished, and the promotion of a man who had been the rebels' own general was a real proof of the clemency of his government, but Joab's envy made the keeping of it turn out ill for them both.

Why Amasa then missed his three days is answered four ways. Keil and Delitzsch suppose the men of Judah distrusted him and were slow to answer his summons. Ellicott alone argues from a geographical detail: since Amasa is met on his return at Gibeon, he must have gone clear out of Judah into Benjamin and spent the time by exceeding his instructions — which, he says, raises great doubt of his fitness for the place promised him, and he notes that Joab will presently insinuate the man was not really loyal. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) offers a choice of two, that the people were worn out by the late war and unwilling to begin another, or that the soldiers had more affection for Joab than for their new general. Henry and Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) put it down to backwardness, Clarke that the muster proved harder than expected and Henry that most men love a loyalty, like a religion, that is cheap and easy.

Passing over Joab is read as policy by all of them, but with different objects. John Gill (reformed) has David unwilling to say anything at all to a man he had removed from his posts for killing Absalom — and records that Josephus has him address Joab after all, flatly against the words of the text. Henry sharpens it: David meant to mortify and degrade him, not so much, he suspects, for the blood of Abner, which Joab shed basely, as for the blood of Absalom, which he shed justly and honourably; and he borrows bishop Hall on how slippery the stations of earthly honour are. Wesley reads a forward-looking caution, that giving the command to Joab would have let him recover his place, leaving Amasa discontented and David's good faith in question. Ellicott states it simply as a determination to pass him over.

The reason David gives for haste is itself disputed. The English has it that Sheba must not reach fortified cities and escape us, which Ellicott notes follows the Latin while the original is difficult and doubtful; others render it that he will pluck out our eye, meaning do us great harm, and the Greek that he will overshadow our eye, which may mean either cause us anxiety or hide where he cannot be found. Keil and Delitzsch come down firmly for the eye: the figure is the apple of the eye used elsewhere for a man's most precious possession, so the sense is that Sheba will do serious injury, and they hold that the gentler reading, that he will withdraw from our sight, cannot be grammatically sustained — crediting the explanation to Böttcher. Ellicott adds a note on the force that went out, Joab's own corps following his brother readily, with the Cherethites and Pelethites and that body of heroes drawn chiefly, he thinks, from the companions of David's outlaw years. Gill and Wesley observe that Joab, though stripped of the generalship, still had a regiment at his back, and went along watching his opportunity.
8:
Everything turns on how the sword came to be in Joab's hand. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) has it contrived down to the fittings: the coat girded close so as not to hang in the way, the belt over it so the weapon lay ready, and the sword set in a sheath too large for it, so that a shake would spill it out as though by accident. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reconstructs the same design more soberly — a dagger stuck in the girdle so arranged as to fall as he advanced, picked up naturally in the left hand while the right went out in greeting, so that no movement raised suspicion. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agrees it was contrived, that at the least motion of his body the sword should drop. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) describe the mechanism without imputing the plan, construing the clause to mean that the sheath came out of the sword-belt and the weapon fell to the ground. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) alone preserves a rival account, that some of the versions and able critics take the words to mean Joab stumbled, the sword falling as he tripped, and that he then took it up left-handed as a man with no bad intention would.

What he struck is also disputed against the English. Clarke holds that the word rendered the fifth rib means any part of the abdominal region, citing the Greek for the groin and the Targum for the thigh, and says that in plain English Joab ripped up his belly; Ellicott glosses it simply as the abdomen. Clarke adds, from his own experience, that a man may live some hours after such a wound, which fits John Gill (reformed) having Amasa still alive and rolling in the road, and Clarke notes in passing that in the East it is the beard, not the man, that is kissed.

Henry anatomises the murder under six heads: it was done subtly and by contrivance, not on a sudden provocation; treacherously, under the pretence of a kinsman's greeting; impudently, before the whole army, by a man too hardened in blood to blush; at a single blow; in contempt of the commission David had given, so that the king was struck at through Amasa's side; and unseasonably, when they were marching against a common enemy and needed to be unanimous. Ellicott reaches the same verdict in one line, that the real motive here, as with Abner, was personal jealousy and ambition. Both he and Keil and Delitzsch remark on the oddity of Joab's appearing among the force at all, and as its commander, without any previous mention; Ellicott supposes he either came out with Abishai or joined him on the road, and that he resumed his old place after the killing with his brother's connivance.

The aftermath is managed. Gill has the man posted by the body on Joab's orders, to reconcile the troops to the deed and keep them moving; Clarke renders the cry as a plain statement that there is now no other commander, and Joab is steadily attached to David, so let the loyal follow him; Ellicott hears in it a suggestion that Amasa had rightly been put to death for his doubtful loyalty; Wesley makes it a straight choice between Joab and a perfidious rebel. On why no one avenged him, Wesley and Henry both point to Joab's standing with the soldiers, who had no kindness for a man lately general of the rebel army, while Ellicott thinks the people — probably the very levies Amasa had been raising — were simply paralysed at the sight. Henry and Wesley close alike, that covering blood with a cloth cannot stop its cry to God for vengeance.
14:
Who it is that goes through all the tribes is the first question. John Gill (reformed) takes it of Sheba, canvassing for a party or else fleeing from place to place, and reports the minority against himself: Josephus understands it of Joab pursuing him, and the Syriac and Arabic versions and R. Isaiah read it the same way, though Gill judges the first sense more generally received. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) and Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) agree on Sheba, Henry adding that he found the tribes less willing on second thoughts than they had been in a sudden provocation, so that he gathered only a few like himself — one bad man, as he puts it, will find or make more.

On the city they converge and then diverge on detail. All place it in the far north: Henry in the lot of Naphtali, Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) on the confines of Syria, Wesley on the northern border toward that part of Syria called Maachah, which is why the longer name distinguishes it from other Abels. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) is the most precise, identifying it with a village still standing north-west of Lake Huleh whose byname celebrates the excellence of its wheat, noting that the preposition in the English should be dropped, and that elsewhere it is called Abel of waters to distinguish it. Clarke alone reaches forward to the gospels, supposing it the capital of the district Luke calls Abilene (Luke 3:1). Sheba's followers divide them three ways: Henry and Wesley make the Berites men of Beeroth in Benjamin, Sheba's own tribe and perhaps his own town; Ellicott calls them apparently a northern clan otherwise entirely unknown, observes that the Greek and Latin seem to follow a different text, and reports the conjecture that the word is a form of the term for fortresses — which he rejects, since no such form is known.

The siege works are disputed on a point of engineering. Clarke denies that the word rendered bank means a bank at all, taking it for a battering engine or a tower from which archers and slingers could work while others sapped below, and arguing that a mere mound could not be described as standing in the trench. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) keep the rampart, piled until it rose level with the town-moat and its low wall; Wesley keeps it too, as a platform for battering or shooting; and Ellicott explains the trench as the space between the city wall and the lower outer wall, so that planting the mounds there was already a decisive advantage.

Then a woman speaks from the wall, and Henry makes more of her than anyone. He notes that not one of the men of Abel, none of its elders or magistrates, offered to treat even at the last extremity — whether from stupidity, or fear of Sheba, or despair of terms — and that this one woman's wisdom saved the city; from which he argues that souls know no difference of sexes, that though the man be the head it does not follow that he has the monopoly of the brains, and that the treasure of wisdom is no less valuable for being lodged in the weaker vessel. Wesley follows him closely in the same judgment. Gill compares her with the woman of Tekoah and reports the supposition of some that she was the city's governess, which Clarke states as probable outright. Keil and Delitzsch find in her opening proverb the evidence that Abel had long been celebrated for the wisdom of its inhabitants, and explain the plural in her self-description by her speaking throughout in the city's name as well as her own.
18:
Her opening is a proverb, and what it means divides them. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) judges the simplest reading the true one, that Abel had become proverbial for its wisdom, but preserves an older Jewish interpretation taken up in the Targum which turns the words into a reproach: has Joab done what the law requires, and asked the city for peace before attacking it (Deut. 20:10)? Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes that second sense from the margin and makes it her tacit rebuke, that the besiegers ought to have demanded the traitor first and the matter would have ended there. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) keep to the reputation for wisdom, Wesley expanding it into the practice of neighbours agreeing to stand by the arbitration of the men of Abel. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) is the most sceptical: the proverb's origin is unknown, much must be supplied to make it speak sense, and though Abel was probably famed for wise men he goes no further.

When she calls herself peaceable and faithful, the witnesses agree she is not speaking only for herself. John Gill (reformed) reads it of a city made up of men peaceable among themselves and faithful to their king, never concerned in any rising, not even the late one. Clarke thinks she speaks in the city's name throughout, and that a mother in Israel means a chief city of a district rather than anything about the speaker; Wesley explains the usage, that great cities are called mothers as the towns depending on them are called daughters. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion from the grammar, since a singular pronoun carries a plural predicate. Wesley also presses the case that she held office: the work was commonly men's, but women were sometimes employed in government, as Deborah judged Israel (Judg. 4:4) — and Clarke infers from the promise she makes that she had great sway in the city's counsels.

Joab's answer draws out the one thing the witnesses find consistent in him. Keil and Delitzsch say her words made an impression and that he felt the truth of her reproach. Henry observes that a man who had lately destroyed Amasa in a private quarrel would not, acting as a general, bear the imputation of delighting in bloodshed. Ellicott quotes the judgment that his character comes out strongly here — politic, decided, bold and unscrupulous, yet never needlessly cruel or impulsive or even revengeful, so that no life is safe which stands in his way while from policy he never sacrifices the most insignificant life without a purpose. Henry draws the practical moral from the misunderstanding on both sides: the city held out believing he aimed at its ruin, he attacked believing the citizens were Sheba's confederates, and both were wrong, so that a great deal of mischief would be spared if contending parties would understand one another.

The terms are then a single head. Keil and Delitzsch note that the hill country named extended south into Benjamin, which is how a Benjamite came to be called a man of those mountains; Ellicott explains it the same way, while Wesley supposes a place within Benjamin so named from the border or from some Ephraimite exploit there. Clarke remarks that beheading was then the punishment of a state rebel, as it still is. Gill has her go down from the wall, convene the chief inhabitants and carry them by the force of her speech; Keil and Delitzsch say she came to them with the very counsel she had given Joab and which he had accepted. Henry adds that Joab, knowing the traitor's face, looked no further and wanted none of Sheba's adherents punished, so the trumpet sounded a retreat and he returned with the trophies rather of peace than of victory.
23:
The chapter ends on a list, and the first name in it is the one that needed explaining. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) says simply that Joab kept the command, being too great to be displaced. John Gill (reformed) is less sure he was ever out of it, offering both accounts — that David meant to remove him and could not, for his influence with the people; or that he had removed him, as parts of this chapter suggest, and found it advisable to restore the man who had just put down the rebellion. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) states it without softening: Joab had murdered Amasa and seized the supreme command, and David was obliged to continue him and dared not call him to account without risking civil war. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reaches the same conclusion from the two successful campaigns, which had so fixed his interest in the army that the king could not safely displace him.

Why there should be a second list at all is answered two ways. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) give a source-critical account: the second section of David's history closes with a roll of ministers as the first did, and the historian kept both lists because they belong to different periods and supplement one another, as the differing names show. Gill reads it as narrative, that naming Joab occasioned an account of the rest, the more so because this was a kind of beginning of the reign again after the risings were quelled. Both note what is new. Keil and Delitzsch count two additions against the earlier roll, the officer over the tribute and a confidential counsellor in the place of David's own sons; Henry picks out the first as the one office erected since, remarking that only toward the latter end of his time did David begin to raise taxes, and that the man who held it held it long and lost his life in it at last (1 Kings 12:18).

What that office was is disputed. Gill makes it revenue from his own people together with tribute from the conquered nations; Clarke calls him chief receiver of taxes, a chancellor of the exchequer; Henry calls him treasurer. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) dissents: the word should rather be rendered the levy, meaning the forced labour which Solomon afterwards employed on so great a scale, and he finds it remarkable that neither the earlier list nor its parallel in Chronicles shows any trace of the post — a feature of eastern despotism introduced only at the close of David's reign and carried much further by his son. He adds that men of nearly the same name held it under Solomon and at the next reign's beginning, perhaps all one person or one family.

The last name is the obscurest. Gill canvasses three identifications — the Ithrite of the roll of heroes, or the son of Ikkesh of Tekoah as the Targum has it, or, his own preference, a descendant of Jair of Gilead who was perhaps a friend to David during his time there — and reports an etymology deriving the name from a root meaning to enlighten. Ellicott refuses the first outright, allowing that an Ira the Ithrite stands among the thirty and seven but finding no ground for identifying the two men. On the title Clarke notes that the Hebrew is literally a priest to David, which the Latin, Greek, Syriac and Arabic all follow, while the Chaldee makes him a prince or chief; he guesses a domestic chaplain, comparing the seers the kings of Judah kept. Keil and Delitzsch make him a confidential counsellor, and Ellicott observes that the post had earlier been filled by David's own sons, so that the murder of the eldest, Absalom's rebellion and death, and the other disorders of that household had apparently forced a change.
